# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–40 (Updated 2026-10-13, Final Revision 20)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Winter of tenth year after Waterloo (1831). Story spans from Sunday, 26th April dinner (Chapters 1–35) through Chapter 36 (winter into summer) to Chapters 37–38 (spring/early summer) to Chapter 39 (autumn) to **Chapter 40 (winter; Imperial dinner day, Monday).**
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Bruton Street, Queen's Gate, Islington, City Road Music-Hall, Cannon Street Hotel, Euston Square, Liverpool, Conservative club in the City, Mount Street, Bond Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Southend; Harrowgate; Lowestoft; Dunholt; Staveton; Gulton; Salford; Yarlton; Salwick; Beccles (Suffolk); coastal towns; rural areas (Sheep's Acre Farm, Salmere, Mirecombe, Miremere); harbor towns (Staveton, Salwick); Coldcombe hill farms; Commercial Road.

## Major Deaths
John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt, Wevie Lindner (died winter, buried Salmere). Conar Hollett (drowned crossing estuary at Gulton; no body seen; Halan Hollett reported it at inn). Feten Lindner followed her to Harrowgate within the month (likely died).

## Rebecca's Arc
Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon) receives allowance but refuses to see her. Appears wealthy at Bath/Cheltenham, busies herself with piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
Married at Ostend; Amelia initiated encounter. Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; daughter Jane his pride.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Welbeck Street resident. Authored "Criminal Queens." Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review; praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" (Mr. Broune). Rejected Mr. Broune's proposal via letter; full of regrets; in debt. Overdrawing her account at bank. Chapter 39: Discovered Felix's failed elopement plan; helped him to bed early morning Wednesday after he arrived drunk. Suffering over his involvement with Marie Melmotte's elopement, money owed. Confessed troubles to Mr. Broune (Thursday evening). Received his counsel: must rid herself of Felix, extract money story, send word to him early next morning. Sent letter to Mr. Broune with Felix's account: claims Melmotte owed him £600; received £250 from Marie via Didon; lost this money at play. Acknowledged she cannot justify believing her son's account.

**Felix Carbury**: Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway. Won substantial sums at gaming. **Chapter 38–39**: Received £250 from Didon Monday 4 P.M.; understood he must go to New York. Planned passage Tuesday under name "Walter Jones"; attempted to meet Ruby at Music Hall but she did not appear. Between 6–7 A.M. Wednesday knocked at Welbeck Street door, drunk and sodden. Remained in bed through Friday morning. **Still in London as of Chapter 40.** **Chapter 40: Marie realizes Sir Felix has not come for her; questions his pluck and truthfulness.**

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit (too young, age disparity). Paul returned "as still dear friend" within week, promising not to see her three months. Wore rose from Roger's room. Roger declared love anew; determination unshaken. Paul thoroughly in love with her. Chapter 39: Turned matter over in mind regarding marriage to one man while loving another.

## Marie Melmotte and Elopement Attempt

**Chapter 38**: Sat up all night packing treasures with Didon. **6 A.M. Wednesday: Robert departed first with big boxes. Marie and Didon followed in second cab. Reached Euston Square, obtained tickets in French, departed. ELOPEMENT INTERCEPTED AT LIVERPOOL PLATFORM.** Gentleman addressed her by name; insisted they return to London; telegraphed Grosvenor Square during journey. Marie taken home; boxes to follow.

**Chapter 39**: Melmotte held her very hard, shook her while speaking. Marie determined: "I'd do it again to-morrow if I had the chance." Melmotte angry at Sir Felix beyond measure; would prosecute if possible. Received £250 back from Mr. Broune. Wrote to Lord Nidderdale, making clear breast of matter; urged him to renew suit.

**Chapter 40**: Nidderdale renewed suit in drawing-room at Grosvenor Square. Marie passionately rejected him: "If we had cared for each other they couldn't have broken it off... You never cared for me a bit." Broke down sobbing, confessed loves Sir Felix Carbury more than any person in world. Upon leaving, Nidderdale reflected he had "prospered, considering the extreme difficulties," thought her "quite a different sort of girl." Marie afterward walked about room almost in dismay, realizing Sir Felix not entirely as nice as thought him; questions why he does not come, why he does not show pluck, why he does not tell truth.

## Paul Montague and Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle

**Chapter 39**: Paul wrote to Mrs. Hurtle acknowledging circumstances made their lives too different for happy marriage; broke engagement before knowing this girl; no grounds for hoping love will lead to results. **Mrs. Hurtle's Response**: Suffered many injuries; this worst, most unpardonable, most unmanly. Called him coward, false liar. Desired him to come with horsewhip in hand; threatened to whip him till has not breath in body. **Paul Meeting**: Paul shown into Mrs. Hurtle's room. Mrs. Hurtle very calm but quietness assumed; could convert into violence at any moment. Spoke softly, then raised voice about his changing mind. Said: "I should still take you, Paul,--still take you; with a confidence that I should yet win you to me by my devotion." Asked advice what to do next; has no home; Mrs. Pipkin's room more her home than any other spot. Asked: "You are in some degree responsible,--are you not,--for my loneliness?" **Paul suggested she remain here; does good to Mrs. Pipkin. Mrs. Pipkin went into hysterics yesterday when Mrs. Hurtle spoke of leaving. Then absolute silence for minute. She handed him sheet containing threat of horsewhip, then handed him scrap written at Lowestoft—softer letter. She said: "Nay, I would not hurt you,--not at this moment... There, you have seen them all. Which will you have?" Paul knelt. She said: "But it will be when you have left me... You do not love me." She put hand upon his forehead, pushed back his hair. Asked: "I wonder whether that other woman loves you... Tell me one thing. When you spoke of--compensation, did you mean--money?" **After Paul left, Mrs. Hurtle announced standing upright: "Everything is over between me and Mr. Montague." She has decided to depart from Islington.**

## Augustus Melmotte and Imperial Reception

**Chapter 39**: Fast asleep in Grosvenor Square Wednesday morning, ignorant of elopement plot. Interrogated Marie about cheque; held her very hard, shook her. By two o'clock matter known to everybody. Anger against Sir Felix infinitely more bitter than against his daughter. Invited Lord Nidderdale to lunch at Conservative club; urged him to visit Grosvenor Square Sunday morning to renew suit.

**Imperial Reception Confrontation**: Stood directly in way of Secretary of State, demanded presentation to Emperor. Insisted: "It is generally understood... that the Emperor is to do me the honour of dining at my poor house on Monday." Threatened: "There shall be no dinner. I'll be d---- if any of the lot shall dine in Grosvenor Square on Monday." Under secretary Lord De Griffin intervened; Melmotte followed. **Had gained his point. In carriage, was intolerable.**

**Imperial Dinner (Chapter 40 - EVENING)**: **Servants and workmen giving admittance; wreaths of flowers and green boughs being suspended. Father Barham made his way to banqueting hall. Melmotte very angry indeed. Had been given to understand he was to sit opposite to Emperor. Now explained to him this could not be done. Melmotte's own seat became really quite obscure. Succeeded in having removed the bar which had been specially put up to prevent his intrusion on his own guests in his own house. Insisted Lord Alfred sit next to himself, having had the objectionable bar removed and his own chair shoved one step nearer to the centre.**

**Critical Issue at Dinner**: Melmotte repeatedly asked Lord Alfred why many guests were absent, glancing round the hall with anxiety. Lord Alfred replied surly: "I tell you I know nothing. I could not make them come." Melmotte's questions were frequent and imperious; Lord Alfred warned: "If you go on making a row, I shall go away." Melmotte told him to "Just sit quiet and let the thing go on. You'll know all about it soon enough." Melmotte rose and moved down the hall behind the guests. **Melmotte knew from the old man's manner (and Lord Alfred's manner) that there was something each could tell him if he would, but he was unable to make the men open their mouths.** Said to Mr. Beauclerk: "It's very odd that gentlemen should promise to come and then stay away. There were hundreds anxious to be present whom I should have been glad to welcome, if I had known that there would be room. I think it is very odd." Pressed Beauclerk about particular men: "Mr. Killegrew and Sir David Boss, and the whole lot. I made a particular point of their coming. I said I wouldn't have the dinner at all unless they were to be asked... I have their answers, saying they'd come." Asked if it was about the election to-morrow. **It became clear to Mr. Beauclerk that Melmotte knew nothing about the forgery rumours that had caused the absences.**

**The Dinner Proceeds**: **The grand arrivals were fairly punctual, and the very grand people all came. The unfortunate Emperor, with impassible and awful dignity, was marshalled into the room on the ground floor. Melmotte, bowing to the ground, walked backwards before him. Princes had all shaken hands with host; Princesses had bowed graciously. Nothing of the rumour had been whispered in royal palaces. The company was very select. The Prime Minister, one archbishop, two duchesses, and an ex-governor of India were alone there. The remainder of the company, under the superintendence of Lord Alfred, were received in the drawing-room above. Everything was going on well.**

**Father Barham's Visit**: Father Barham walked close to scene of action. "Who the d---- are you?" Melmotte asked. Father Barham stood humbly with his hat off. "I am the Rev. Mr. Barham," said visitor. "I am the priest of Beccles in Suffolk." Melmotte: "And what may you want?... Where the mischief are the fellows, Alfred, who ought to have seen about this?" **Father Barham went away disgusted; yet not altogether disheartened. Man had not declared he was not Roman Catholic. Before he returned to Beccles, Father Barham made himself believe Mr. Melmotte was certainly Roman Catholic.**

**Melmotte's Charitable Maneuvering**: Presented hundred guineas towards erection of altar for new church of St. Fabricius. Donation accompanied by letter leaving little doubt that new member for Westminster would be member of Catholic party in House. Mr. Alf's newspaper bit at this, noting apparent hypocrisy with Protestant support. **Melmotte possessed only by belief that England's glory demanded his return for Westminster; thoroughly ignorant of political questions, political history, Parliament's working; had never read a book in his life; yet fully confident England demanded Melmotte for Westminster. Perhaps most remarkable circumstance was fact that he came almost to believe in himself.**

## FORGERY RUMORS AND THE PICKERING PROPERTY CRISIS (Chapter 40 - CRITICAL DEVELOPMENT)

**The Rumor's Spread (Monday, Chapter 40)**: Horrid rumours prevailing in the City and spreading westwards to the House of Commons. Word "forgery" whispered by more than one pair of lips. Rumour particular in its details: inferred the forgery to Melmotte's mode of acquiring the Pickering property. Nature of forgery described in various ways, as was signature said to have been forged. Many believed, or almost believed, something wrong had been done; some great fraud committed.

**Details of Pickering Property Transactions**: **Pickering estate had been already mortgaged by Melmotte to its full value at an assurance office. In such a transaction nothing dishonest; but as this place had been bought for the great man's own family use, and not as a speculation, even this report of the mortgage tended to injure his credit.** Other tidings told as day went on: **Houses in the East-end of London were said to have been bought and sold, without payment of the purchase money as to the buying, and with receipt of the purchase money as to the selling. Squercum himself had seen the letter in Mr. Bideawhile's office which conveyed to the father's lawyer the son's sanction for the surrender of the title-deeds. That letter, prepared in Mr. Bideawhile's office, purported to have Dolly's signature.** Signature, though scrawled as Dolly always scrawled it, was not like the scrawl of a drunken man.

**Squercum's Investigation**: Squercum quite sure that his client had not signed the letter. **Dolly's manner on this occasion qualified to convince. "Yes," he said to Squercum; "I know when I'm lack-a-daisical and when I'm not. Awake or asleep, drunk or sober, I never signed that letter." And Mr. Squercum believed him.**

**How Rumour Spread to the City**: Though elder Longestaffe first heard of matter only on previous Saturday, **Mr. Squercum had been at work for above a week. Squercum's little matter alone might hardly have attracted the attention given on this day to Melmotte's private affairs;--but other facts coming to light assisted Squercum's views. A great many shares of the South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway had been thrown upon the market, all of which had passed through the hands of Mr. Cohenlupe;--and Mr. Cohenlupe in the City had been all to Mr. Melmotte as Lord Alfred had been at the West End.** Then there was the mortgage of Pickering property, for which the money certainly had not been paid; and traffic with half a street of houses near the Commercial Road, by which a large sum of money had come into Melmotte's hands. **It might all be right. There were many who thought it would all be right. But it was felt to be a pity that Mr. Melmotte was not in the City.**

**Impact on Imperial Dinner Attendance**: **The Lord Mayor had made up his mind that he would not go to the dinner. As his lordship remarked, Melmotte was a commercial man, and as these were commercial transactions it behoved the Lord Mayor of London to be more careful than other men.** Others of the chosen few of the City resolved upon absenting themselves unless the Lord Mayor went. **No less than six declared City defaulters. At the last moment a seventh was taken ill and sent a note to Miles Grendall excusing himself.**

**Political Leadership Response**: **Prime Minister stated: "I should not feel myself justified in acting upon such a report... The dinner must certainly go on."** Political antagonist declared with a smile that at such a crisis he would not desert his honourable friend;--but he could not answer for his followers. Strong feeling among leaders of Conservative party of distrust in Melmotte. **At that moment even the Prime Minister was much disturbed in his mind; but in such emergencies a Prime Minister can only choose the least of two evils. To have taken the Emperor to dine with a swindler would be very bad; but to desert him, and to stop the coming of the Emperor on a false rumour, would be worse.**

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway
Railway from Salt Lake City through New Mexico/Arizona into Mexico, terminating Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles. Stock at par; shares sold at premium. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not building railway. Directorate: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague.

## Lord Nidderdale and Marquis of Auld Reekie
That absurd elopement perhaps his strongest objection. "What does it matter, if the money's there?" Marquis seemed to think escapade had simply been the girl's revenge. **By the Sunday evening he had determined that he would try again. Expected plum would fall into his mouth.** Perhaps Marquis had been wrong in flying at wealth reputed to be almost unlimited, but which was not absolutely fixed. Couple of hundred thousand pounds down might have been secured with greater ease. But here was prospect of endless money.

## Roger Carbury and Father Barham
Nearly forty. Never owed shilling he couldn't pay. Firmly opposed Melmotte connection on principle. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless. Declared love to Henrietta anew; determination unshaken. **Chapter 39: Philosophical Discussion with Bishop: Roger discussed Melmotte's fitness for Parliament. Argued: "Men reconcile themselves to swindling... It seems to me that the existence of a Melmotte is not compatible with a wholesome state of things in general." Bishop countered: existence of Melmotte not necessarily pernicious if he would vote Conservative; country is changing.** **Father Barham at Carbury Manor**: Roof blown off Father Barham's cottage by wind; Roger offered him shelter while damage being repaired. Shelter much more comfortable than priest's own establishment; Father Barham in clover.

## Georgiana Longestaffe and Mr. Brehgert

**Chapter 40**: Georgiana asked Lady Monogram whether she would have Mr. Brehgert (presumably Jewish) to dinner. Lady Monogram declined, stating she maintains social lines and does not introduce "new-comers." Explained: "I don't make the lines; but there they are; and one gets to know in a sort of way what they are." Compared having Mr. Brehgert to inviting the butcher round the corner or the hair-dresser, saying "I don't feel inclined to risk my own reputation on the appearance of new people at my table." However, offered compromise: Georgiana could ask Mr. Brehgert to Tuesday evening gathering when rooms would be full. "So the matter was at last settled. Miss Longestaffe did ask Mr. Brehgert for the Tuesday evening, and the two ladies were again friends."

**Georgiana's Reasoning**: Georgiana reflected: "Lovers with all the glories and all the graces are supposed to be plentiful as blackberries by girls of nineteen, but have been proved to be rare hothouse fruits by girls of twenty-nine. Brehgert was rich, would live in London, and would be a husband. People did such odd things now and 'lived them down,' that she could see no reason why she should not do this and live this down. Courage was the one thing necessary,--that and perseverance. She must teach herself to talk about Brehgert as Lady Monogram did of Sir Damask." Remembered how she and Julia Triplex had scattered scorn upon some poor girl who had married a man with a Jewish name, whose grandfather had possibly been a Jew.

## Minor Characters and Details
Didon (Marie's attendant, executed elopement plan). Miles Grendall (Secretary to Melmotte; does not pay debts of honour; thrust note of City defaulter into his hands just as Emperor arrived). Robert (Marie's servant; departed 6 A.M. Wednesday with big boxes). Lord Alfred Grendall (absolutely dependent on Melmotte; born and bred gentleman; found position almost insupportable). Dolly Longestaffe (parent of forgery rumor via attorney Squercum). Village characters: Aessa, Ellan Lindner, Manelle, Nylis Corrett, Elnelle Lindson, Cotho Hollwood, Ilrald Hollwood, Gamira Brackwood, Ortho Corrett, Rorine. Harbor town scenes: Gulls, salt and tar smells, wind off water.
